## Part 1 · 00:00

[00:00] Hi, I'm glad you could join me in my study. The last time we were together, I argued that it is logically incoherent to accuse God of acting immorally or unjustly in punishing Christ for our sins. Since on a divine command theory of ethics, whatever God does is right since God's own will and commands determine what is right and wrong. These commands are not arbitrary but are rooted in his divine nature. So God can do whatever he wants so long as it is consistent with his divine nature.

[00:47] And it seems to me that the substitutionary atonement of Christ for our sins is perfectly compatible with God's loving and compassionate and holy nature. So this objection to penal substitution based upon the unjustness or immorality of substitutionary punishment seems to me not even to get off the ground given the coherence of a divine command theory of ethics. Perhaps the best spin that the objector might put on this objection is to say that it is part of the divine nature to exercise retributive justice.

[01:30] That retributive justice itself belongs to the nature of God and therefore God must act in accordance with the axioms of retributive justice. Now, this requires us to look more closely at theories of retributive justice because those who present this sort of objection rarely penetrate below the surface to examine theories of retributive justice. Theories of retributive justice can either be positive or negative. The heart of retributive justice lies in a positive theory. That the punishment of the guilty is justified because they deserve it. That is the heart of retributive justice.

[02:12] It is the positive thesis that the guilty deserve to be punished. There is also a kind of negative retributive justice which says that only the guilty should be punished. That is to say that the innocent should not be punished. Well, in that case, how do we know that what is essential to the nature of God is not simply positive retributive justice. The Bible says that God will in no wise clear the guilty that he will punish sin and therefore God is a positive retributivist.

[03:00] But if God chooses to relax the demands of retributive justice so as to allow Christ to be punished in our place, who's to say that that's inconsistent with his nature? Even if it belongs to God's nature to establish a negative system of retributive justice for human beings where whereby human beings may not punish one another substitutionarily or even that God will not punish a human being substitutionarily for another. What's to prevent God himself from entering into human history and from himself bearing the punishment for our sins?

[03:43] So it seems to me that we can say that God does have as part of his essential nature positive retributive justice, but he is only qualifiedly a negative retributivist in that while he does not allow negative uh retributive um justice to be meed out on on innocent persons, nevertheless that would allow God himself self to punish Christ for our sins because Christ is a divine person, not merely a human person.
